result.reason: The enabling of Firebase on a Google Cloud project. Once Firebase has been added to a project it cannot be removed from it. Firebase is Google's backend platform for mobile and web apps. A Firebase project and the registration of an Android or Apple app in it hold the identity of the app (package name or bundle id, signing hashes, team id) and the API key through which the app reaches Firebase services. STACKIT has no mobile or web application backend platform: none of the 115 resource types of the pinned STACKIT provider is one (0 hits for firebase in resource names, descriptions and attributes, checked 2026-11-05), and the product list at docs.stackit.cloud/products/ (read 2026-11-05) names none. The registration itself therefore has nothing to move to; a person decides, app by app, which backend replaces the Firebase services the app uses.
review: List the Firebase services each app uses (authentication, database, storage, messaging, remote config); each needs its own replacement.
The signing keys and store listings stay with Google Play and the Apple App Store; only the backend the app talks to moves.

result.reason: A topic maps to a RabbitMQ exchange and each subscription to a bound queue. Publishers and subscribers switch from the Pub/Sub client to AMQP; acknowledgement deadlines, retries and dead-letter topics map to acknowledgements, requeueing and dead-letter exchanges. STACKIT also publishes a PubSub API (beta) with topics and pull subscriptions, for which the STACKIT provider has no resource: the draft states it as the candidate beside the RabbitMQ instance, behind the opt-in of the beta API, as calls of the execution plan, and what the API has no field for (push delivery, filters, dead-letter topics, ordering, a customer-managed key) is a step of its own. The RabbitMQ instance is the path carried out until that opt-in is accepted; accepting it makes PubSub the target of the topic instead, never both.
result.validated_against: terraform-provider-stackit@0.116.0; docs messaging/rabbitmq 2026-09-23; STACKIT catalogue eu01 2026-09-24 (RabbitMQ 4.1); checked 2026-11-05: the pinned provider schema 0.121.0 holds no pubsub resource (0 hits), stackit-api-specifications services/pubsub holds v1alpha and v1beta (the repository embeds v1beta in data/stackit/api-specs/pubsub_v1beta.json: topics, pull subscriptions, publishers and subscribers; no push, filter, dead-letter, ordering or encryption field)

result.reason: A Google service account becomes a STACKIT service account named after its account ID (shortened to the STACKIT name rules, so its e-mail address changes and every reference to it is updated). What the account may do is what the IAM resources of the estate grant it, and the draft carries that where it can show the mapping: a grant to the account on a project, a folder or an organisation becomes a STACKIT role assignment of the account. The role is written as it is only where the Google role has a STACKIT role with the same permissions or fewer on a project; every other role is an input without a default that names the candidates and how they differ, because a wider role is never a default. A grant that lets another account act as this one becomes an Act-As assignment. Grants that cannot be written are listed in the draft with the reason: a condition (a STACKIT role assignment has none), a policy document, a repeated grant, a role or a member that is not visible statically, and a member that is a person, a group or the identity of a Kubernetes workload. An additive grant (a member) adds one member and removes none, as a role assignment does; a binding or a policy removes every member of its role that it does not list, a role assignment never removes anyone, and the draft marks each such grant. The workloads that ran as the account are not attached to it by this block; workloads that got credentials from the metadata server or GKE Workload Identity need explicit STACKIT credentials or a federated identity. Keys are never carried.

result.reason: Secrets move to STACKIT Secrets Manager (a Vault-compatible KV store). Applications switch from the Secret Manager client to a Vault client or to injection by the platform (e.g. External Secrets Operator on SKE); IAM accessors become Secrets Manager users (read-only or read-write for the whole instance) or, narrower and experimental, role bindings on a secret group.

findings.message: The secret has grants for individual principals. Access on STACKIT Secrets Manager is coarser than a Secret Manager grant: a Secrets Manager user is read-only or read-write for the whole secrets engine of its instance, with no scope to one secret or path. Narrower access exists only as role bindings on the instance or on a secret group (a named list of secrets) in the alpha API of the service, and the pinned provider offers them as resources of its experimental IAM feature (stackit_secretsmanager_instance_role_binding_v1 and stackit_secretsmanager_secret_group_role_binding_v1), which its documentation says may change or be removed; the specification does not list the roles a secret group accepts. A grant of one Google principal on one secret therefore cannot be carried one to one: decide per principal whether it gets a user of the whole instance, a role binding on a secret group of the secrets it may read, or a separate Secrets Manager instance.
root: source-provider-unverified:google

result.reason: A Cloud Build trigger starts a build when a source event happens (a push or a pull request on GitHub, Bitbucket Server, a repository of the 2nd generation, Developer Connect or Cloud Source Repositories), when a Pub/Sub message arrives, when a webhook is called or when a person runs it. The build is a list of container steps (a build block, or a file in the repository) with substitutions, images and artifacts to push, secrets from Secret Manager, a service account, a log destination and optionally a manual approval. STACKIT has no trigger or build resource. The same delivery is a workflow of STACKIT Git Pipelines (workflows written for GitHub Actions; STACKIT-managed or custom runners; secrets from STACKIT Secrets Manager or the repository; a manual-approval action) or the customer's own CI/CD. Nothing is converted: the trigger conditions (branch and tag expressions, file filters, the event kind), the steps (a container step becomes a step or a job with a container), the secrets (created again, never copied), the service account (replaced by the credentials the workflow uses against STACKIT), the log destination and the approval are written again by a person. The pages read describe pipelines that run when changes are pushed; other events (pull requests, schedules, manual runs) are verified against the Forgejo Actions reference.
review: Write the workflow in the repository: one job (or step) per build step, with the same container images or their STACKIT equivalents.
Recreate every secret the build reads in STACKIT Secrets Manager (read with the vault action) or as a repository secret; the values of the source are never copied.
Write the trigger conditions again as the on: section of the workflow and verify each event kind against the Forgejo Actions reference.
Decide where images and artifacts go: the package registry of STACKIT Git takes container images from any OCI client, or keep your own registry, and change the image names in the deploy steps.

target.service: STACKIT Object Storage as origin of a STACKIT CDN distribution, with a custom domain

result.reason: A Firebase Hosting site: the unit of hosting, whose identifier builds the Firebase-provided sub-domains, optionally associated with a Firebase web app. Firebase Hosting is Google's web hosting with a global CDN: a site holds versions (the files with the rewrites, redirects and headers of firebase.json), releases publish a version on a channel, preview channels expire by themselves, and custom domains get a certificate. STACKIT has no web hosting service of this kind (0 hits for firebase in the resource names, descriptions and attributes of the 115 resource types of the pinned STACKIT provider, checked 2026-11-05; the product list at docs.stackit.cloud/products/ read 2026-11-05 names none), but it has the parts for static content: Object Storage buckets, and a CDN whose distribution can use a bucket as its origin and takes redirect rules, TLS settings and a WAF (the stackit_cdn_distribution resource of the pinned provider is a beta resource), with custom domains. Rewrites to Cloud Run services or Cloud Functions, preview channels and the release history of a site have no counterpart there. Static files are published into an Object Storage bucket by a pipeline; a CDN distribution with the bucket as origin serves them on a custom domain, and the redirects of firebase.json become redirect rules of the distribution. Preview channels and release history are rebuilt in the pipeline (one bucket path per preview). Rewrites to dynamic backends need a load balancer or another origin, which a person decides.
review: Check the rewrites, headers and clean-URL settings of firebase.json: redirects have a counterpart in the CDN, rewrites to a backend do not.
Plan the DNS change for the custom domain and the certificate that the CDN issues for it.

result.reason: A Google service account becomes a STACKIT service account named after its account ID (shortened to the STACKIT name rules, so its e-mail address changes and every reference to it is updated). What the account may do is what the IAM resources of the estate grant it, and the draft carries that where it can show the mapping: a grant to the account on a project, a folder or an organisation becomes a STACKIT role assignment of the account. The role is written as it is only where the Google role has a STACKIT role with the same permissions or fewer on a project; every other role is an input without a default that names the candidates and how they differ, because a wider role is never a default. A grant that lets another account act as this one becomes an Act-As assignment. Grants that cannot be written are listed in the draft with the reason: a condition (a STACKIT role assignment has none), a policy document, a repeated grant, a role or a member that is not visible statically, and a member that is a person, a group or the identity of a Kubernetes workload. An additive grant (a member) adds one member and removes none, as a role assignment does; a binding or a policy removes every member of its role that it does not list, a role assignment never removes anyone, and the draft marks each such grant. The workloads that ran as the account are not attached to it by this block; workloads that got credentials from the metadata server or GKE Workload Identity need explicit STACKIT credentials or a federated identity. Keys are never carried.
